direct_answer: Spinal stenosis is a narrowing in the spine that can press on nerves, often linked to osteoarthritis. It can cause leg pain, numbness or heaviness when walking or standing, which often eases by sitting or leaning forward. Planned rest stops, walking aids and exercise can help.
author: Louis Maxwell

content:
Many people with spinal stenosis find they can walk only so far before their legs ache and they need to sit.

This guide covers walking with planned stops. It is educational information, not a diagnosis or personal treatment plan.

Why walking can be hard

Narrowing in the lower spine can press on nerves. Symptoms often come on with walking or standing and ease with sitting or bending forward.

Planning walks

  • Know where seating is.
  • Use a walking aid with a seat if advised.
  • Leaning on a trolley can ease symptoms.
  • Walk little and often.

Exercise and treatment

A physiotherapist can suggest exercises. Your GP can review pain relief and refer you if needed.

Standing with spinal osteoarthritis

  • Standing still, such as in a queue, can be harder than walking.
  • Sit to prepare food, or rest a foot on a low step.
  • Plan rest stops when you go out.
  • Ask a physiotherapist about posture and pacing.

When to get help

  • Call 999 or go to A&E if you have new numbness around the bottom or genitals, or problems controlling your bladder or bowels.
  • Get urgent advice if leg weakness is getting worse.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Is a walking aid giving in?

No, it can help you go further.

Will surgery be needed?

Most people are managed without surgery.
